briefing.headline: The simulation predicts that a four-day week at full pay would roughly halve leaving over the next 12 months, from 779 to 398 leavers out of 5,000 (-49%). Treat the size of that drop as an upper-end, directional estimate.
briefing.most_at_risk: Long commuters gain most (-57% leaving, versus -45% for short commuters) because they get a whole commute day back, and managers gain least (-47%) because they expect to carry the burden of proving output holds on 32 hours.
risks: Nearly every voice, including the most enthusiastic, warns that 'keep output the same' could quietly become cramming five days into four, so burnout and resentment could build during the trial.
Finance and operations staff specifically flag month-end close and output measurement, and managers expect to absorb the pressure, so the policy could backfire for the people asked to police it.

The predicted retention benefit runs over 12 months, but the trial lasts six. Withdrawing the policy, or leaving its future unclear, could erase the gain and turn the goodwill into a sense of something taken away.
design_changes: Before launch, agree with each team what 'same output' means in concrete measures, and name the low-value work and meetings that will stop, so the trial does not rely on longer, denser days.
Give month-end-heavy and operational teams a flexible arrangement, such as staggered days off or a movable day during close, and give managers explicit support and authority to adjust workloads.
Say now how and when the decision to keep, change or end the policy will be made after six months, and check workload and wellbeing through the trial, not just output.
briefing.confidence: low, because the 48 modelled voices are strikingly uniform and positive, the gaps between groups are only a few points and may be noise, and only the direction (a large drop in leaving) is a reasonable read, not the exact 49%.
